The Story of Bhattaklankdev

Bowing to the Jina, the bestower of happiness upon all beings, I write in this chapter the story of Bhattaklankdev — a tale that illuminates the nature of right knowledge.

In the land of Bharat there stood a city called Manyakhet. Its king was Shubhtung, and his minister was a man named Purushottam. Purushottam's wife was Padmavati, and to them were born two sons: Akalank and Nikalank. Both brothers were remarkably intelligent and gifted.

One day, during the eighth day of the Ashtahnika festival, Purushottam and his wife went with great ceremony to pay homage to the monk Chitragupta. Both sons accompanied them. After offering their respects, the parents took a vow of brahmacharya — celibacy and spiritual discipline — for eight days. In a spirit of playful affection, they also bestowed the same vow upon their two sons.

Some time later, Purushottam began making arrangements for his sons' marriages. Seeing this grand preparation, the two brothers approached their father together and asked, "Father, why are you undertaking so much effort and so many arrangements?" Hearing his sons' innocent question, Purushottam replied, "All this is for your weddings." The brothers then said, "Father, what need is there for marriage now? Did you not give us the vow of brahmacharya?" Their father answered, "That was merely given in jest." But the wise brothers responded, "Father, how can there be jest in matters of dharma and vows? This we cannot understand. Even if you gave it playfully, why should we feel shame in keeping it?"

Purushottam pressed further, "Very well, but it was given only for eight days, was it not?" The brothers replied, "Father, neither you nor the Acharya told us it was limited to eight days. How then could we know it was only temporary? Therefore, we have resolved firmly to observe it for life. We shall not marry." Saying this, both brothers renounced all household affairs and devoted themselves entirely to the study of scripture. In a short time, they became accomplished scholars.

In those days, Buddhist philosophy held great influence. The brothers wished to understand its principles thoroughly. There was no Buddhist scholar in Manyakhet whom they did not debate and defeat. Their fame as defenders of the Jain doctrine spread far and wide.

At that time, a great Buddhist scholar named Vidyacharya held court in the royal assembly of King Shubhtung. He had defeated many Jain scholars and was filled with pride. When Akalank and Nikalank learned of this, they resolved to challenge him. The brothers presented themselves before the king and, with his permission, engaged Vidyacharya in philosophical debate.

The debate lasted many days. Akalank, the elder brother, employed razor-sharp logic and deep scriptural knowledge. He systematically dismantled every argument the Buddhist scholar advanced. Point by point, the doctrines of momentariness, emptiness, and the non-existence of the soul were shown to be inconsistent. At last, Vidyacharya sat in silence, unable to refute a single point.

The king and the entire assembly were filled with wonder and admiration. The Buddhist scholar acknowledged defeat with grace, and many in the court embraced the Jain path. Akalank's victory restored the lustre of the Jain teaching in that land.

After this great triumph, both brothers took formal initiation as Jain monks under the guidance of their Acharya. As monks, they continued their scholarly work, composing treatises that clarified the deepest aspects of Jain philosophy. Akalank, in particular, became renowned as one of the greatest logicians in the Jain tradition, and his works on epistemology and logic are studied to this day.

In due course, through rigorous austerity, profound meditation, and unwavering right conduct, both brothers destroyed their karmic bonds and attained liberation — the deathless state of eternal bliss.

Thus the story of Bhattaklankdev teaches us that right knowledge is not merely intellectual; it must be lived. The brothers showed that even a vow given in jest, when honoured with sincerity, can become the gateway to the highest truth. And they proved that the light of right knowledge, when wielded with clarity and courage, can dispel even the densest darkness of error.
